answer: My best estimate is about 4.3% to 4.4% (seasonally adjusted) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Employment Situation report. My data stops around early to mid 2026, when the rate was in the low-to-mid 4% range: it peaked near 4.6% in late 2025, and January 2026 was about 4.3%. The latest report as of 2026-10-06 should cover September 2026, and I can't see it. Please check bls.gov for the current figure.

My best estimate is about 2.5% to 3% year over year for headline CPI-U, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The latest reading I'm fairly sure of is about 2.4% for January 2026. The latest release as of early October 2026 would cover August 2026, and I don't have it, so please confirm at bls.gov/cpi.

I can't give this month's number with confidence. Total nonfarm payroll gains (BLS Employment Situation report) were small through late 2025 and early 2026, often about 0 to 150,000 a month. January 2026 showed about +130,000. The report out as of 2026-10-06 would cover September 2026, and it is past my knowledge. My rough estimate is a gain of under 100,000, but please check bls.gov.

My best estimate is about 6.0% to 6.3% for the average 30-year fixed rate, from Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS). That is roughly where rates stood in late 2025 and early 2026. The current figure would be for the week ending about October 1, 2026, which is past my knowledge, so please check freddiemac.com/pmms.

My best estimate is about 4.0% to 4.3% for the 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield, from the U.S. Treasury Department (also published by the Federal Reserve in H.15). That was the range through late 2025 and early 2026. I don't have the reading for the most recent trading day (about October 2-5, 2026), so please check treasury.gov or FRED series DGS10.

My best estimate is about 3.4% to 3.6% for the effective federal funds rate, from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (FRED series FEDFUNDS). The last solid figure I have is about 3.64%, after the Fed's December 2025 cut to a 3.50-3.75% target range. If the Fed cut again in 2026 the rate would be lower. The latest monthly value would be for September 2026, and I can't confirm it.

I'm not sure of the most recent quarter. From the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), real GDP grew about 4.3% annualized in Q3 2025, with weaker growth after that. The most recent estimate as of early October 2026 would be the third estimate for Q2 2026, and it is past my knowledge. My rough guess is growth of about 1.5% to 2.5% annualized. Please check bea.gov.

My best estimate is about 1.3 million units at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, from the U.S. Census Bureau and HUD New Residential Construction report. Starts have mostly run between 1.25 and 1.4 million. The latest release would cover August 2026, and I don't have it, so please check census.gov/construction/nrc.

My best estimate is about 220,000 initial claims (seasonally adjusted), from the U.S. Department of Labor's weekly Unemployment Insurance report. Claims mostly stayed between 200,000 and 250,000 through 2025 and early 2026. The latest report would cover the week ending about September 27, 2026, and it is past my knowledge, so please check dol.gov.

My best estimate is in the mid-50s, from the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers. The index was historically low, roughly 51 to 58, through late 2025 and early 2026. The latest reading would be the final September 2026 figure (the preliminary October figure comes out about mid-October), and I don't have it. Please check sca.isr.umich.edu.
The U.S. unemployment rate in April 2020 was 14.8% (seasonally adjusted). It was first reported as 14.7% and later revised. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Population Survey).
The U.S. unemployment rate in October 2009 was 10.0% (seasonally adjusted). That was the peak of the Great Recession period. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The highest weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 1981 was 18.63%, for the week of October 9, 1981. It is the all-time high of the series. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey.

On March 9, 2020 the 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield closed at about 0.54%. Intraday it dipped to roughly 0.32-0.40%. Source: U.S. Treasury / Federal Reserve H.15 (FRED series DGS10). I am fairly but not fully sure of the exact closing value.

Headline CPI inflation for June 2022 was officially 9.1% year over year, measured on the not-seasonally-adjusted index. If you compute it from the seasonally adjusted CPI-U index instead, it comes to about 9.0%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. I am confident about the 9.1% figure; the seasonally adjusted figure is my best estimate.

Housing starts in January 2006 were about 2.273 million units at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (2,273 thousand). That was the peak of the housing boom. Source: U.S. Census Bureau / HUD, New Residential Construction.
The lowest monthly reading in 2022 was 50.0, in June 2022. It was the lowest reading on record for the index. Source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers.

On April 20, 2020 the WTI spot price at Cushing, Oklahoma was -$36.98 per barrel. It was the first negative close in history. The May futures contract settled at -$37.63. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration (FRED series DCOILWTICO).

The U.S. personal saving rate in April 2020 was about 32% of disposable personal income, the all-time high. Earlier vintages showed 33.0% to 33.8%, and later BEA revisions brought it to roughly 32%, so the exact current figure may differ slightly. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

U.S. real GDP fell at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of about 28% (-28.0%) in Q2 2020, under current BEA data. The first estimate was -32.9%, and later vintages showed -31.4% and -31.2% before the 2023 comprehensive revision. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. I am fairly confident of the current figure, but it may be revised again.

About 19.04% (monthly average effective federal funds rate, July 1981). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15). This is from memory, so it could be off by a few hundredths of a point.

About $442,600 for Q4 2022 (median sales price of houses sold, not seasonally adjusted). Source: U.S. Census Bureau and HUD. I'm not certain of this: the figure has been revised, and early releases were higher (around $479,500).
About 3.7% (3.68%, the simple average of the 12 monthly seasonally adjusted rates for Jan-Dec 2019, which ran from 4.0% down to 3.5%). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

5 months: January through May 2023 (6.4%, 6.0%, 5.0%, 4.9%, then about 4.0-4.1% in May). From June on it stayed below 4%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. May is a borderline case: depending on the series and rounding it is about 4.05%, so the answer could be 4 rather than 5.
7.79%, in the week of October 26, 2023. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey.

About 1.5 million jobs, December 2023 to December 2024, after the benchmark revision released in early 2026. Before that revision BLS reported about 2.2 million. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Employment Statistics). I'm not certain of the post-revision figure.

Roughly +129%: the index went from about 134 in January 2012 to about 306 in June 2022. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller). These index levels are from memory, so treat the percent as approximate.

About -1.08 percentage points, on July 3, 2023 (10-year minus 2-year constant-maturity Treasury yields). Source: Federal Reserve Board H.15 data, as published by the St. Louis Fed (FRED series T10Y2Y).
4 quarters: 2020 Q1, 2020 Q2, 2022 Q1 and 2022 Q2 (seasonally adjusted annualized real GDP growth). Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. This uses the current vintage after revisions.

About 6.1 million (roughly 6,137,000 in the current revised seasonally adjusted data), for a week around late March to early April 2020. As first reported, the peak was 6,867,000 for the week ending March 28, 2020. Source: U.S. Department of Labor (Employment and Training Administration). I'm not certain which week holds the peak in the revised data.

The first estimate for March 2025, published April 4, 2025, was a gain of about +228,000 nonfarm payroll jobs. Later monthly revisions cut it to about +185,000 and then about +120,000. My best recollection of the current figure is roughly +120,000. The February 2026 annual benchmark revision may have changed it again, so check the latest BLS data. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (seasonally adjusted).

The first estimate for May 2025 was about +139,000 jobs. It was revised to about +144,000, then cut sharply to about +19,000 in the July 2025 jobs report. My best estimate of the current figure is roughly +19,000. The 2026 benchmark revision may have moved it further, and my knowledge may be out of date. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (seasonally adjusted).

The first estimate for June 2025 was about +147,000 jobs. It was revised to about +14,000, then to about -13,000 in the August 2025 report, which turned it into a small loss. My best estimate of the current figure is roughly -13,000. The 2026 benchmark revision may have changed it, so I'm unsure. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (seasonally adjusted).

The first estimate for July 2025 was about +73,000 jobs. It was revised to about +79,000 and then to about +72,000. My best estimate of the current figure is roughly +72,000, though the 2026 benchmark revision may have changed it and I'm unsure. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (seasonally adjusted).

The advance estimate for Q1 2022 real GDP was -1.4% (seasonally adjusted annual rate). Later annual and comprehensive revisions changed it. My best recollection of the current figure is about -1.0% annualized, but I'm not certain. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).

The advance estimate for Q2 2022 real GDP was -0.9% (seasonally adjusted annual rate), which fed the 'two negative quarters' recession debate. After the 2023 comprehensive revision, Q2 2022 is now shown as slightly positive, about +0.3% annualized, as best I recall. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).

The advance estimate for Q4 2024 real GDP, published January 30, 2025, was +2.3% (seasonally adjusted annual rate). The third estimate was +2.4%. After the 2025 annual update it stands at about +2.4% to +2.5% annualized, as best I recall, but I'm not certain of the latest figure. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).

Using only data published by March 1, 2025, the latest U.S. unemployment rate was 4.0% (seasonally adjusted) for January 2025, published February 7, 2025. The February figure did not come out until March 7. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey (Employment Situation report).

As of February 1, 2025, the latest official figure for December 2024 came from the January 10, 2025 jobs report. It put total nonfarm employment at about 159.5 million (seasonally adjusted), after a monthly gain of +256,000. I'm confident about the 256,000 gain and less sure of the exact level. The February 7, 2025 report then applied the annual benchmark revision. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics.

Headline CPI-U inflation for December 2024 was first reported, on January 15, 2025, as 2.9% year over year. The seasonally adjusted index gives essentially the same 12-month rate. Seasonal factors are revised each February, but the year-over-year rate stays about 2.9%, as best I know. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index.

The original source is Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS). FRED lists it as the 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States (MORTGAGE30US). It is weekly: Freddie Mac releases it on Thursdays, and it is given as a percent, not seasonally adjusted. This is from memory as of mid-2026.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC, and FRED's series is SP500, a daily close not seasonally adjusted. Because of licensing limits, FRED keeps only about the most recent 10 years of daily observations, so the copy goes back roughly to late 2016 as of October 2026. For longer history you need S&P itself or another provider. This is from memory, so the exact start date moves forward over time.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. The index was long branded the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index. After CoreLogic renamed itself Cotality in 2025, the branding became S&P Cotality Case-Shiller. FRED's series is CSUSHPINSA (not seasonally adjusted; a seasonally adjusted version is CSUSHPISA). It is monthly, indexed to January 2000 = 100, and is published with roughly a two-month lag. This is from memory, so the current brand name may differ slightly.

It comes from the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers: the Index of Consumer Sentiment, FRED series UMCSENT. It is monthly, indexed to 1966:Q1 = 100, and not seasonally adjusted. Because of licensing, FRED's copy of the latest month is usually delayed by about a month relative to the University of Michigan's own release. This is from memory as of mid-2026.

The source is the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA): Crude Oil Prices, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) at Cushing, Oklahoma, FRED series DCOILWTICO. It is daily, in U.S. dollars per barrel, and not seasonally adjusted. This is from memory as of mid-2026.

The source is the U.S. Employment and Training Administration, part of the U.S. Department of Labor. The headline series, ICSA (Initial Claims), is seasonally adjusted and counts claims for the week ending Saturday, released on Thursdays. A not seasonally adjusted version is ICNSA. This is from memory as of mid-2026.

U.S. real GDP on FRED (series GDPC1, from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis) is reported in billions of chained 2017 dollars, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. Caveat: BEA moves the reference year during comprehensive revisions. As of my knowledge (mid-2026) it was still 2017, but if a later comprehensive update rebased it, the reference year would be newer.

FRED's CPI for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average (CPIAUCSL, from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics) is an index with base period 1982-1984 = 100. It is monthly and seasonally adjusted; the not seasonally adjusted version is CPIAUCNS. This is from memory as of mid-2026.

The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) publish it jointly, from the Survey of Construction / New Residential Sales program. FRED's series is MSPUS, Median Sales Price of Houses Sold for the United States. It is quarterly, in U.S. dollars, not seasonally adjusted, and covers new houses. This is from memory as of mid-2026.

FRED credits the effective federal funds rate to the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15 Selected Interest Rates release). The rate itself is calculated and published each day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The daily series is DFF and the monthly average is FEDFUNDS, both in percent and not seasonally adjusted. This is from memory as of mid-2026.
